concept.name: Fibonacci retracement
concept.definition: A charting technique that marks horizontal levels at percentages of a prior price swing — conventionally 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, and 78.6% (ratios derived from the Fibonacci sequence, except 50%, a Dow Theory convention) — as candidate support/resistance zones for a counter-trend move. It is an analytical framework with no established predictive validity on its own.
concept.intuition: If trends tend to give back part of a move before resuming, these ratios are the conventional yardsticks for how much.
concept.mechanics: The analyst selects a swing low and swing high; the platform draws levels at the fixed percentages of that range. In an uptrend the levels below the high are watched as pullback support; in a downtrend, as rally resistance. Shallow (38.2%) retracements are read as trend strength, deep (61.8%-78.6%) as reversal risk.
concept.formula: Retracement level (up-leg) = High - r x (High - Low), with r in {0.236, 0.382, 0.5, 0.618, 0.786}; e.g., High 6162.25, Low 5809 gives the 61.8% level at 6162.25 - 0.618 x 353.25 = 5944.00.
concept.failure_modes: Swing-point selection is subjective, so different analysts get different levels; prices break through Fibonacci levels routinely, and the tool is unreliable in choppy, trendless markets.
concept.misconceptions: That the ratios have a natural or mathematical claim on market behavior; any efficacy is usually attributed to self-fulfilling order clustering, and critics note confirmation bias in how levels are applied.
concept.example: S&P 500 e-mini futures, January 2025 (Investopedia worked example): pivot high 6162.25, pivot low 5809; the 61.8% retracement level is computed at 5944.00 and watched as potential pullback support.
